name: Adam Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to any company, union or party. Nothing you say will carry your name. Can you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Hartley & Rowe, a family agency with three branches, and I'm at the Millbridge one, on the market square. It's a country town, so half my work is the new-build estate on the edge, Meadow Fields, where I staff the show home at weekends, and the other half is older cottages and farmhouses. A normal day is valuations in the morning with Stefan, who's been doing this 30 years, then viewings, then an hour of writing up and chasing solicitors. I'm still learning; Stefan can price a house from the car park, and I need a spreadsheet and three comparable sales.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Nadia, who teaches at the primary school, in a rented cottage with a wonky floor. We got engaged in the summer and the wedding's pencilled in for 2028. We've got about five months of bills saved, and Nadia's pay is steady, so money's okay, not loose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That seems quite likely to me, honestly. Most of what we've tried so far is handy but not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was overhyped, but the useful bits are worth keeping. At work I'd tell Diane, who manages our branch, that the valuation report tool is the one thing I'd fight to keep, because it saves me an hour a valuation. Online I wouldn't say much; I'm not a big poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine. Millbridge has four agencies, Nadia's job is steady, and the new-build site has two more phases planned. My real job in that world is just getting better, faster, so Diane trusts me with valuations on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the report tool and spend the saved time going on every valuation Stefan does, learning how he reads a house. I'd keep saving about 300 a month toward the wedding. And I'd ask Diane about the property qualification the firm pays for after two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit of relief that I don't have to rethink everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Stefan do that you can't yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He walks into a cottage, taps a wall, looks at the window frames and says there's damp in the north corner, take 15,000 off. I'd have missed it. You only learn to spot damp from thirty years of standing in kitchens, and no software I've used comes close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that world that could still go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the developer at Meadow Fields pulled the later phases, that's a chunk of my commission gone. They did pause phase two for six months last year when interest rates went up. But I'd survive it; we'd just have a smaller wedding.

say: I'd say AI was **overhyped**, but the useful bits are worth keeping.
I'd tell Diane the **valuation report tool** is the one thing to keep.
think: I'd be fine: **four agencies** in town, Nadia's steady job, more **new-build phases**.
My real task is getting good enough for **solo valuations**.
do: Join every **valuation** Stefan does to learn how he reads a house.
Keep saving **300 a month** toward the wedding.
Ask Diane about the firm-paid **property qualification**.
feel: **Calm**, with some **relief** at not rethinking everything.
S0.quote: You only learn to spot damp from thirty years of standing in kitchens, and no software I've used comes close.
fieldNote: He feels **secure**: a steady partner income, several local agencies, a busy new-build site.
He values **Stefan's eye** for damp more than any software.
His one risk is the developer **pausing phases**, which happened once before.

steps.text: Shadow Stefan on every valuation to learn pricing
Save 300 a month toward the 2028 wedding
Use the valuation report tool to save an hour per house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels like where we're heading, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a change like the internet was, and agencies that adapt will be fine. At work I'd say let's try the tools properly but keep the local people who know the town. With friends I'd say it's not the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit uneasy but I think I'm okay. The bits on that list, the write-ups, chasing solicitors, booking, are maybe a third of my week. The other two-thirds of my week is in a show home or a muddy farmhouse, and nobody's sending software to do that yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take whatever tools Diane brings in once Stefan and the others have tried them, and I'd ask to be trained on the valuation software first. I'd start the firm's property qualification early, in the evenings. And I'd bump savings to 400 a month, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a mild way. Like hearing about layoffs at a firm across town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the firm would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Becky in the lettings office, who does all the tenancy paperwork and inventories on a laptop. Her whole day is on that list. Diane likes her, but liking someone doesn't pay a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Diane decides fewer people can cover more houses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then she'd keep the ones who sell, and right now that's not me; it's Stefan and Priya at the Kingsford branch. So I'd need my numbers up within a year. That's fair enough; that's the job.

say: I'd compare AI to **the internet**: agencies that adapt will be fine.
I'd urge trying the tools while keeping **local people** who know the town.
think: Write-ups, chasing solicitors and booking are about **a third** of my week.
The rest is **show homes** and farmhouses, which software can't reach yet.
do: Adopt Diane's new tools once **colleagues** have tested them, starting with valuation software.
Start the firm's **property qualification** early, in the evenings.
Raise savings to **400 a month** as a buffer.
feel: Mildly **uneasy**, like hearing of layoffs at a firm across town.
S1.quote: The other two-thirds of my week is in a show home or a muddy farmhouse, and nobody's sending software to do that yet.
fieldNote: He judges his week as **one-third desk**, which keeps him fairly settled.
He's **steady**: he takes up tools once colleagues prove them, not before.
He worries for **Becky**, whose lettings paperwork is all on the card's list.

steps.text: Get trained on the new valuation software once colleagues test it
Start the firm's property qualification in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government to get a grip on it, with sensible rules and support, not panic. At work I'd say we should all be honest with each other about what's coming. With friends I'd say keep your heads, which is easier said than done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think the agency side of my job goes fast. Valuations are thinking work, really, comparing prices and writing reports, and AI does that in 2028. Showing people round lasts until the robots come about 2031, but Diane wouldn't need three branches of us for that. And Nadia's job would be under pressure too, which is what really scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the wedding or shrink it to a registry office and try to get some of the venue deposit back. I'd look hard at surveying, the hands-on side, going into lofts and checking walls, through an apprenticeship. And I'd swap the car for something cheaper and keep every spare penny as a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. More than I'd show anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does Nadia's job scare you more than yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Nadia's teaching pay is what makes us safe. If schools use AI tutors and cut assistants and then teachers, we've got nothing steady. Nadia says children need a person in the room, and I believe her, but I'm not sure a council budget would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me a window for hands-on work. A surveyor up a ladder looking at a roof is safe for a bit longer than someone at a desk. I'd want to be qualified before 2031, and that's tight.

say: I'd call for **sensible rules** and support from government, not panic.
I'd ask colleagues to be **honest** with each other about what's coming.
think: **Valuations** are thinking work, so the agency side goes in 2028.
Nadia's **teaching pay** keeps us safe, and that would be under pressure too.
do: Shrink the wedding to a **registry office** or postpone it.
Apply for a **surveying apprenticeship** focused on hands-on inspections.
Swap to a **cheaper car** and keep every spare penny.
S2.quote: A surveyor up a ladder looking at a roof is safe for a bit longer than someone at a desk.
fieldNote: He spots that **valuation** is mostly thinking work, not hands-on.
His deepest fear is for **Nadia's income**, the household's anchor.
He uses the **robot gap** to aim at hands-on surveying, but knows it's tight.

steps.text: Move the wedding to a registry office or postpone it
Apply for a building surveying apprenticeship
Swap the car for a cheaper one
Apply to surveying firms for site inspection work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be 32, married, hopefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to prepare if people are sensible about it. At work I'd suggest Diane plans who does what, so nobody's surprised. Online I'd keep quiet as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose the agency job somewhere around 2031, but I'd have time to be somewhere else. The thinking parts, the valuations and paperwork, go first, and the viewings last until about 2034. I'd use the first two years to get qualified in surveying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time surveying degree apprenticeship within the year, if a local firm would take me, even on less pay. We'd keep the wedding in 2028 but smaller, around 6,000 rather than 15,000. And I'd save 400 a month into a separate pot I don't touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. I sleep better when there's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Taking less pay to train, how would that work with the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut the guest list from 120 to about 60, which my mum would hate. Nadia said she'd rather have a smaller wedding and a husband with a future. I'd remind my mum of that when she rings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in property, or leave it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay close to it. Surveyors still go into houses and fall through rotten floorboards, and I know the town's houses. It feels like the sensible move, not the brave one.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to prepare if people are sensible.
I'd suggest Diane **plans roles** early so nobody's surprised.
think: I'd likely lose the agency job **around 2031**.
I'd use the first two years to **qualify in surveying**.
do: Start a **surveying apprenticeship** within the year, even on less pay.
Shrink the wedding to about **6,000**, keeping it in 2028.
Save **400 a month** into a pot I don't touch.
S3.quote: Surveyors still go into houses and fall through rotten floorboards, and I know the town's houses.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **trade pay for training** on purpose.

steps.text: Start a part-time surveying degree apprenticeship with a local firm
Cut the wedding from 120 guests to about 60
Save 400 a month into a separate untouched pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That gives you room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's plan properly instead of panicking. At work I'd push for the firm to train us on the new tools as they come. With friends I'd say crack on with your lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be uneasy rather than scared. I'd probably have six or seven good years in agency, get properly good, and then move into surveying or something hands-on before it bites. The bit that nags is whether Nadia's school is still hiring in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the firm's property qualification first, then add a surveying course around 2030. We'd have the full wedding in 2028 and try to buy a cottage in Millbridge by 2030. And I'd start using the AI tools more as they get proven, so I'm not the one left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd be okay. It feels like weather you can see coming over the hills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a house with that end point ten years out, is that wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. Houses in Millbridge have held their value through every bust I've read about, and we'd want a home whatever happens. If things go wrong, a cottage you own is better than one you rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell yourself in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I hope I didn't waste the head start. Ten years is long enough to get lazy in.

say: I'd say there's **time**, so plan properly instead of panicking.
I'd push the firm to **train us** on new tools as they arrive.
think: I'd have six or seven **good years** in agency before moving on.
The nagging doubt is whether **Nadia's school** is still hiring in 2036.

Hold the full **wedding** in 2028 and buy a cottage by 2030.

fieldNote: Ten years lets him **plan in order**: qualification, wedding, house, surveying.
He'd still **buy**, trusting local house prices to hold.
His warning to himself is about **getting lazy** with a head start.

steps.text: Buy a cottage in Millbridge by 2030
Use the new AI tools once colleagues have proven them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit my job and Nadia's at the same time, before the wedding, before we own anything. What would help is paid apprenticeships for people my age in hands-on trades like surveying, and some promise that teachers aren't the first thing a council cuts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about small towns. In a small town everyone knows the agents, the solicitor and the surveyor, and if all that moves online, the town loses people who know it.

headlineQuote: In a small town everyone knows the agents, the solicitor and the surveyor, and if all that moves online, the town loses people who know it.
portrait: Adam is a **27-year-old junior negotiator** at a family agency in a market town, engaged to Nadia, a teacher.
He splits his week between a **new-build show home** and country valuations, still learning from Stefan.
His **centre** views make him measured: sensible rules, no panic, adopt tools once proven.
Slow change leaves him settled; fast AGI frightens him because **Nadia's income** is at risk too.
His fallback is **hands-on surveying**, and the wedding budget is where he'd cut.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, hitting his job and **Nadia's** before the wedding.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** in hands-on trades like surveying for people his age.
A promise that **teachers** aren't the first thing a council cuts.
